questions.stem: What does it mean for a reaction to be reversible?

options.text: It occurs in both directions, with the products able to reform the reactants
options.explanation: Both directions run; nothing about the reaction is one-way.

options.text: It can be undone only by changing the temperature
options.explanation: Reversibility is built into the reaction itself, not a switching condition.

options.text: It runs halfway and stops there permanently
options.explanation: Reversible reactions do not stop; equilibrium is a balance of ongoing reactions.

options.text: It produces the same amount of products as reactants
options.explanation: Amounts at equilibrium need not match; rates, not quantities, are equal.

questions.stem: Why must equilibrium be reached in a closed container?

options.text: So none of the participating species can escape and nothing else can enter
options.explanation: The closed vessel keeps every participant present so the two reactions can balance.

options.text: To keep the pressure high enough for the reaction to start
options.explanation: Starting the reaction is not the issue; keeping every species in the vessel is.

options.text: To stop the products decomposing
options.explanation: Products decomposing is part of the reverse reaction, not something prevented.

options.text: To keep the temperature constant
options.explanation: The container blocks matter transfer; temperature control is a separate matter.

questions.stem: The concentrations at equilibrium are constant. What does that mean?

options.text: Each concentration stays the same over time, though the two sides' amounts need not match
options.explanation: Constant means unchanging, not identical between reactants and products.

options.text: Reactant and product concentrations are equal to each other
options.explanation: Equality of concentrations is not required; only the rates are equal.

options.text: Both concentrations are zero because the reaction finished
options.explanation: The reaction has not stopped; both sides remain present.

options.text: The concentrations keep rising steadily
options.explanation: Rising is change; constant means no net change over time.

questions.stem: Why is the equilibrium described as dynamic?

options.text: Because both reactions keep running constantly, converting molecules into each other at the same rate
options.explanation: Dynamic names the ongoing change that balances out.

options.text: Because the concentrations change slowly over time
options.explanation: Concentrations stay constant at equilibrium.

options.text: Because the reaction needs constant stirring or heating
options.explanation: No input is required; the balance maintains itself.

options.text: Because the molecules move faster once equilibrium is reached
options.explanation: Molecular speed is not the claim; the ongoing two-way reactions are.

questions.stem: A leak develops in the reaction vessel and gas escapes. What happens to the equilibrium?

options.text: It is disturbed: escaping material means the system is no longer closed, so the balance cannot hold
options.explanation: The closed-system requirement is exactly about keeping everything in the vessel.

options.text: Nothing; equilibrium survives leaks because the rates stay equal anyway
options.explanation: With material leaving, the two rates can no longer stay matched.

options.text: The reaction immediately runs to completion
options.explanation: Loss of material unbalances the rates; it does not force completion.

options.text: The reaction reverses completely, leaving only reactants
options.explanation: Nothing forces total reversal; the balance is simply lost.

questions.stem: State the condition on the two reaction rates that defines equilibrium in a reversible reaction.
questions.modelAnswer: Equilibrium is reached when the rates of the forward and reverse reactions become equal.

questions.stem: State the system condition a reversible reaction needs before equilibrium can be reached.
questions.modelAnswer: A closed system is required, so no species can leave the vessel and nothing can enter.

questions.stem: Explain why a reversible reaction reaches equilibrium instead of running to completion.
questions.modelAnswer: Because a reversible reaction runs in both the forward and reverse directions: as products build up the reverse reaction runs faster, until the two rates become equal at equilibrium.

questions.stem: A student claims that a reaction mixture at equilibrium must contain equal amounts of reactants and products. Use what stays constant at equilibrium to answer the claim.
questions.modelAnswer: The claim is wrong: at equilibrium it is the concentrations of reactants and products that stay constant while nothing else changes, which is not the same as saying the amounts are equal.

questions.stem: At the start of the Haber process, why is the forward rate at its highest?

options.text: Because the nitrogen and hydrogen concentrations are at their highest, and rate tracks concentration
options.explanation: The note's own reasoning: the most reactant present means the fastest forward reaction.

options.text: Because the ammonia is pushing the reaction forward
options.explanation: There is no ammonia at the start; only nitrogen and hydrogen are present.

options.text: Because the temperature is highest at the start
options.explanation: Temperature is held steady; the start's speed comes from abundant reactants.

options.text: Because the vessel is newest and cleanest
options.explanation: The rate is set by concentrations, not by vessel condition.

questions.stem: Why does the forward rate fall as the reaction proceeds?

options.text: The nitrogen and hydrogen concentrations gradually decrease as they are consumed
options.explanation: Less reactant means fewer collisions, so the forward rate drops.

options.text: The nitrogen and hydrogen particles slow down over time
options.explanation: Particle speed is not the mechanism; concentration is.

options.text: The ammonia blocks the forward reaction from outside the vessel
options.explanation: Ammonia rises within the mixture; it does not act from outside.

options.text: The vessel walls absorb the gases
options.explanation: Nothing leaves a closed vessel; the fall is internal consumption.

questions.stem: What happens to the backward reaction as ammonia accumulates?

options.text: It speeds up, because its reactant, ammonia, keeps increasing
options.explanation: The reverse reaction consumes ammonia, so more ammonia means a faster reverse rate.

options.text: It stays at zero until equilibrium is reached
options.explanation: The backward reaction begins as soon as ammonia exists.

options.text: It slows down, because the ammonia blocks it
options.explanation: More ammonia speeds the decomposition, it does not slow it.

options.text: It runs faster than the forward reaction until equilibrium
options.explanation: The backward rate rises to meet the forward one; the note has them becoming equal.

questions.stem: Why do the two rates eventually become equal?

options.text: In the closed system the two reactions are interlinked and no gas can escape, so the rates settle at equality
options.explanation: The note's own account: interlinked reactions in a closed system converge.

options.text: Because the reaction runs out of energy and stops
options.explanation: Nothing stops; the rates match while both reactions continue.

options.text: Because the nitrogen and hydrogen have completely run out
options.explanation: Reactants are still present at equilibrium; their concentrations are constant, not zero.

options.text: Because the ammonia fills the vessel and forces a stop
options.explanation: Filling the vessel is not what balances the rates.

questions.stem: At equilibrium in the Haber process, which statement is true?

options.text: The forward and reverse rates are equal, and the concentrations have stopped changing
options.explanation: That is exactly the pair of features the exam hint lists.

options.text: Both reactions have stopped, so the amounts are fixed
options.explanation: The reactions continue; the amounts are fixed by the equal rates.

options.text: The rate of making ammonia equals the total amount made
options.explanation: Rate compares with rate; it is not compared with an amount.

options.text: The concentrations of nitrogen, hydrogen and ammonia are all equal
options.explanation: Equal rates, not equal concentrations, is the equilibrium condition.

questions.stem: State the industrial process used in the note as the example of a reaction reaching equilibrium.
questions.modelAnswer: The Haber process, run in a sealed container.

questions.stem: State the vessel condition under which the Haber process reaches equilibrium.
questions.modelAnswer: It runs in a sealed container, forming a closed system.

questions.stem: Explain why the backward reaction speeds up as the Haber process proceeds.
questions.modelAnswer: Because the ammonia concentration rises as the reaction proceeds, and the backward reaction decomposes ammonia back into nitrogen and hydrogen, so more ammonia means a faster backward reaction.

questions.stem: A sealed Haber vessel has run for several hours: the amounts of nitrogen, hydrogen and ammonia have stopped changing. State which reaction is faster at that moment, the forward or the backward.
questions.modelAnswer: Neither — the two rates have become equal, because equilibrium has been reached.
